outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - master the fundamental techniques of drawing and mode of representation; and - develop own forms of expression

title: Principles of Chinese Calligraphy
description: This course is offered for beginners in Chinese calligraphy. It describes the basic concepts and techniques of Chinese calligraphy, the selection and use of materials and tools, and teaches students the regular, clerical and seal scripts. Students will be prepared for more advanced courses of various scripts.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - manage general knowledge and usage of the four treasures of Chinese studio; - recognize the characteristics of different formats of Chinese calligraphy; and - apply what they learn in the class to the creation of elementary Chinese calligraphy in clerical and regular scripts

title: Principles of Chinese Painting
description: This course introduces the materials and tools, techniques in brushwork, ink tone variations, and colouring to beginning students of Chinese painting. Related skills such as mounting, writing of inscriptions, imprinting of seals will also be explored. Students will practise traditional paintings of pine trees, rocks, bamboo, and human figures, etc., in preparation for in-depth studies in landscape, figure or bird-and-flower paintings.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - understand the content and basic concept of Chinese painting;  - manage basic techniques in brushwork, tone variation and coloring of Chinese painting; and - apply what they learn in the class to the creation of elementary Chinese painting
syllabus: The topics will include: - introduction to materials and tools; - exercise of techniques in brushwork, tone variation and colouring; - knowledge of Chinese painting such as mounting, inscriptions writing, seals stamping; and - studies of four gentlemen, vegetable, figure, pine tree and rock.

title: Fundamentals of 3-Dimensional Forming
description: This course provides students with basic concepts and skills in three-dimensional forming through various material processes, both in traditional handicraft and digital 3D forming environment. Emphasis will be placed on three major aspects: 1) the perception of form and space; 2) materials and construction; and 3) 3D form as artistic expression. The course will also help students to get familiar with studio operations that would equip them for further sculptural practice.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  1. perceive diverse artistic potentials of form and space in daily surroundings;  2. develop ideas and concepts for 3D artistic expression;    3. understand and apply fundamental 3D elements and principles such as form-space-transformation, plane and volume, balance and gravity, scale and proportion, materials and textures etc…; and  4. manage wide range of tools and machinery for 3D construction both in handicraft and digital forming environment.
syllabus: 1. Observing Form & Space Understanding the nature as well as the structure of diverse natural and man-made forms and spaces.  2. Transformation of Form & Space Explore various ways of form-space-transformation that lead to ideas/concepts of 3D artistic expression.  3. From 2D Plane to 3D Form Pattern cutting as a means of analyzing, de-constructing and re-constructing a 3D form.  4. 3D Construction - from Handicraft to Digital Forming and vice-versa Investigate wide range of possibilities to further develop a hand-built sculptural form within a digital environment. Usage of 3D scanner and printer will be introduced and practiced. The final piece should be a combination of hand-crafted and digital forming.  5. The Container & the Contained A tailor-made container / box will be constructed to house the sculptural form developed in the previous stages. Relevant images as well as different materials / textures will be explored and eventually applied onto the container / box to further reference the conceptual development of the sculptural form. Usage of appropriate tools and machinery will be introduced and practiced.

title: Artistic Traditions in China
requirements: Not for students who have taken UGEA1310 or UGED2291
description: (UGEA1310 is double-coded with FAAS1600.) In light of artifacts whether excavated or collected as well as historical texts, this course provides an overview of Chinese art over 5000 years. Through studying the art and culture of the pre-historic era and the Bronze Age, and the development of painting, calligraphy, religious sculpture, architecture, jade, gold, silver, and ceramics throughout the centuries, students will understand the special characteristics and historical development of Chinese art and culture over the centuries. Artistic exchange between China and its neighbouring countries will be given special attention. Tutorial sessions involve practical workshop or the study of actual art objects at the Art Museum.
outcome: After taking this course, students are expected to get a basic understanding of:   1. The origin and development of major artistic traditions in China; 2. The artistic and cultural significance of Chinese art; 3. The achievements and contributions of great masters; 4. The ways of looking at Chinese art; and 5. The relationship between Chinese art and foreign culture.
syllabus: 1. The art and culture of prehistoric and Bronze Age China; 2. Chinese ceramics and other decorative arts; 3. Chinese imperial art throughout the ages; 4. Art of the Chinese literati; 5. Chinese religious art; and 6. Artistic exchange between China and its neighboring countries.

title: Introduction to Art History
description: This course aims to develop students’ abilities to “read” artwork. Students will gain a basic understanding that besides aesthetics and forms, artwork represents the culture, philosophy, religion, technology, literature, and history when it was produced and collected. Critical art historical concepts including but limited to style, mass production, iconography, patronage, narrative, connoisseurship, and forgery, will be used to analyze masterpieces to hone students’ object-based research skills.

title: Life and Arts in Pre-Modern China
components:
Discussion
Exercise
Field Studies/Field-trip
Lecture
Seminar

description: (UGED2316 is double-coded with FAAS2100.)  In the traditional discourse of Chinese painting, it was believed that an artist should “外師造化，中得心源” (outwardly learn from the Nature and inwardly trace the source of their own heart). Unfortunately, with the enormous temporal and geographical difference, both the Nature and the “heart-source” of the ancient masters, as well as their techniques in articulating the two, appear to be unapproachable to us living in the modern age. Likewise, the field’s ambiguous meta-language full of expressions like “氣韻生動” (infusing ch’i to show life movement) or “意趣” (subtle charm resulted from spontaneity) can also be a hurdle to uninitiated students.Distant it might seem, art, after all, is inspired by real life. This course seeks to explore the material basis of the Nature artistically heightened by the ancient artists directed by their “heart-source”. We would try to explore the abstract philosophical ideas and aesthetic ideals by looking at something physical and concrete: by visiting specific scenic sites, we would be able to compare the landscape with the paintings they inspired and have more idea on how the visual vocabulary and grammar of Chinese painting “translates” the real world; and by viewing the objects, or even experience some of the activities central to the artists’ cultural life, students would also have a more substantial understanding on the “heart-source” of these painters.This course would use the Songjiang and Wu Schools of painting as case studies. A field trip will be organized and students will be walked through the areas of Shanghai, Suzhou and Hangzhou where the Ming Dynasty painters were active in. Through the well-preserved tangible heritage of the region, students could have a better feeling of the intangible ideational world of the ancient masters and their artistic pursuits. The endeavours of the local communities in preserving these invaluable treasures will also be reviewed.

title: Reading Chinese Painting
description: (UGED2338 is double-coded with FAAS2101.) Symbols and images that carry traces of Chinese cultural traditions can be found everywhere in the modern world. This course provides a comprehensive overview of the history of Chinese painting and trains students’ abilities in reading images so that they can achieve a deeper understanding of the cultural meanings embedded in everyday encounters. Through a broad survey of Chinese painting from the pre-Song period to the present, students will become familiar with major works, figures, theories, and movements, while also developing fundamental art-historical skills for observing and analyzing images’ style, subject matter, and socio-cultural meaning. In-class discussion of readings and writing exercises will teach students how to read scholarly literature and translate their observations and research on paintings into various forms of writing, such as academic reports, museum labels, or catalogue entries.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  Be familiar with key works, figures, theories, and movements in the history of Chinese painting from antiquity to the present;  Independently analyze the visual features of Chinese painting, including, but not limited to, brushwork, color, composition, and materiality;  Apply major art historical methods, such as formal analysis, iconography, and archival research, to interpret Chinese cultural elements embedded in everyday life;  Identify the distinctiveness and historical significance of Chinese culture through the study of Chinese painting and recognize the importance of preserving cultural heritage and artifacts;  Compose written works, such as academic essays, catalogue entries, and exhibition labels, to effectively communicate their research and insights on Chinese painting and culture.
syllabus: 1. Introduction to the course: Ice breaker This introductory session will guide students through reading selected entries from Maxwell K. Hearn, How to Read Chinese Paintings (The Metropolitan Museum of Art and Yale University Press, 2008), to help them understand the basic formats and relationship between imagery and text in Chinese painting. 2. Figural painting (I): Line This session will introduce major figural paintings from the pre-Song period and examine the historical, cultural, and literary contexts in which they emerged. It also explores the significance of “line” as a fundamental expressive element in Chinese painting. 3. Figural painting (II): Narrative This session will investigate major figural paintings from the Song period onward and analyze the historical and cultural factors that led to the gradual decline of figural painting as a dominant genre in later periods. 4. Landscape painting (I): Style This session will analyze the stylistic characteristics of landscape paintings from northern and southern China prior to the Southern Song period and examine the political and philosophical contexts that contributed to the emergence of this new genre as a representative form of Chinese painting. 5. Landscape painting (II): Text and image This session will explore the relationship between text/poem and image in paintings from the Southern Song period onward, as well as the related yet distinct aesthetic ideals associated with courtly, Buddhist, and literati contexts. 6. Landscape painting (III): Painting schools This session will examine the specific temporal and spatial conditions, political environment, and social structures that contributed to the emergence of Chinese “painting schools” in the Ming and Qing periods. 7. Paintings genres and art collecting This session will examine the importance of art collecting within the Chinese political tradition and survey a range of lesser-known genres of Chinese painting, considering their changing significance within major art collections from the Song period to the present. 8. Bird-and-flower painting: Ink and color This session will examine major bird-and-flower paintings, analyzing their artistic techniques as well as their cultural, political, and literary significance across historical periods. 9. Religious painting (I): Iconography This session will introduce the transmission, visual features, and theological aspects of Chinese Buddhist and Daoist painting, with particular emphasis on the methods and significance of iconographical research. 10. Religious painting (II): Painting workshop This session will explore the workshop practices involved in the creation of Chinese paintings, as well as the political and economic contexts in which they emerged.

title: Arts of Ancient China:Neolithic Through Bronze Age
description: Using artifacts recovered from archaeological excavations, this course will explore the artistic achievements of early China. Students will be introduced to the painted and black pottery and the ritual and ornamental jades from the Neolithic period; oracle bone script, ritual bronze vessels, bronze weapons and musical instruments, painted lacquers, and ritual and ornamental jades of the Bronze Age; as well as the beginnings of contact with nomadic cultures, and pictorial representation in bronze, silk, and clay. Students will emerge with a multifaceted picture of the cultural and artistic legacy of early China, ready for in-depth studies in the arts of the period.

title: Art Along the Silk Road
description: The opening of the Silk Road during the second century BCE marks China’s entry in the international arena of artistic and cultural exchange. Through the study of a wide range of artifacts from the Han through Tang-Liao-Jin-Song periods, this course will examine the results of these exchanges from a variety of perspectives. Students will acquire a balanced and updated understanding of the role played by cultural interaction in China’s artistic development during this period. Contents of this course will vary with instructors and students. Offerings with different subtitles can be taken up for credit, up to a maximum of two times.

title: History of Early Chinese Ceramics
description: This course examines the development and artistic characteristics of Chinese ceramics from the Neolithic period (ca. 5000-2000 BCE）to the Song dynasty. Representative wares such as early painted and black pottery, funerary figurines, stonewares, and high-fired porcelains from major kilns will be discussed. This course also explores the relationship between the ceramics and the social culture of different periods through in-depth analysis of excavated materials from archaeological sites such as tombs, kilns and pagodas. Excavation of ancient Chinese ceramics in Hong Kong will also be included in the survey, with the possibility of field visits to local archaeological sites.

title: Classical Traditions of Chinese Calligraphy
description: Focusing on calligraphy before Song, this course aims at familiarizing students with the origin and development of Chinese calligraphy: oracle-bone script, bronze inscriptions, stele-engravings, and ink works on silk and paper. In-depth discussions of calligraphic works in museum collections and those from archaeological discoveries will lead to an understanding of stylistic development, while different classical traditions created by great masters will be highlighted and evaluated.

title: Visual and Material Culture of the Ming Dynasty
description: (UGEC2391 is double-coded with FAAS2106.) This course discusses the changes of visual and material cultures of the Ming dynasty through studying objects, images and texts. Topics including ceramics, lacquerwares, gold and precious stones, textiles, prints and other art and artefacts made for people from all walks of life will be covered. Through introducing representative images and objects and different trends of social development of the Ming period, such as religious fervor, sumptuous consumption, and erotic culture, the course aims at exploring how the emergence of classic images and artefacts are linked to the political, economic, religious, technological and aesthetic development of a time.

title: Religious Art of China
description: (UGED2306 is double-coded with FAAS2110.) This course aims at exploring the relationship between Chinese art and religion from the Shang period onwards. Students will be introduced to religious paintings, buildings, sculptures, clothes and ritual objects. Through studying important archaeological and extant religious artifacts and recent research on Chinese religious beliefs, students are expected to understand the characteristics and significance of Chinese religious arts. Religious ideas behind different forms of art will also be discussed.

title: Introduction to Asian Art: The Art and Archaeology of West, South, Southeast, and Inner Asia
description: (UGED2315 is double-coded with FAAS2113.) The survey introduces the art and material culture of pre-20th century Asia with particular attention paid to trans-regional and cross-cultural interactions. Select artistic traditions in West (mainly, Iran), South (India, Sri Lanka, and the Himalayas), Southeast (Indonesia, Burma, Thai, Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam), and Inner (Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Mongolia) will be examined against their philosophical, religious, socio-political, economic, aesthetic, and technological backgrounds. Major themes include (1) the rise of civilizations, (2) developments of various artistic forms and media, (3) tombs and funerary paraphernalia, (4) the spread of Buddhism, Hinduism, Islamism, and other worldviews across the region, and (5) Indianization and Sinicization.
outcome: After completing this course, students will be able to:  Acquire rigorous art-historical methods in describing and analysing artistic monuments;  Identify major artistic traditions in pre-modern Asia and their inter-relations;  Think critically about works of art as integral part of a larger visual and material culture;  Explores the ways in which we construct knowledge on traditional Asian culture and society, especially, on the basis of unique modern experience of our era; and  Develop skills in participating in scholarly arguments and writing an academic essay.

title: Art in HK: from the Foundation of the Colony to the Early 21st Century
description: This course provides an overview of the development of art in Hong Kong from the colonial days to the early 21st century, including traditional Chinese painting, calligraphy and seal carving, modern ink painting, and various art forms in western media. It examines the uniqueness of Hong Kong’s art in the context of its economic growth, cultural integration of east and west, and freedom in artistic creation, towards an evaluation of the achievements of Hong Kong’s art in the twentieth century.

title: Global Currents in Contemporary Art
description: (UGEC2371 is double-coded with FAAS2118.) Contemporary art is diverse and expansive, and its timeline, topics, and aesthetic strategies, are continually redefined. This course offers an introduction into political and aesthetic issues addressed in global contemporary art, particularly since 1989 which marked the fall of the Iron Curtain and the first primordial “global” exhibition at Centre Pompidou. It will provide a variety of perspectives to discuss visions of the future presented by artists from diverse cultural backgrounds, who engage with such global issues as migration, borders, postcolonial conflicts, gender perspectives, environmental crisis, biodiversity, and digital capitalism. It will provide students with foundational knowledge on the emergence, developments, and challenges of global contemporary art discourses, as well as their contesting relationship with artistic autonomy and the society. We will examine a range of topics and methods employed by influential artists and thinkers in various geographies. This will provide a toolkit for understanding and curating contemporary art. To put critical thinking into practice, we will integrate exercises such as screenings and discussions, group projects, and exhibition proposals. Beyond art historical perspectives, we will also delve into questions regarding humans’ relationship with each other and the nonhumans, which are fundamental for understanding global currents and crisis addressed in contemporary art.

title: Western Art I: from the 15th to the Late 19th Century
description: This course aims to give a broad overview of Western art from the 15th to the late 19th century. The Renasissance is universally regarded as a fundamental period in the history of Western Art. Subsequent period styles, such as Mannerism, Baroque, Neo-Classicism, Romanticism and Realism are either development from the art principles of the Renaissance or reactions against the rules and bounds developed during this important period. Special attention will be given to the major artworks of each movement as well as the historical events which have influenced the evolution of Western art.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  - know the general timeframe of the developments of Western art from the early Renaissance to the late 19th century;  - situate an artwork (sculpture, painting and architecture) within a time period: for example, recognize whether a painting is a High Renaissance or a work of the Romantic period; and - understand the historical background of each period.

title: Creative Watercolour Painting
description: This course is an introduction to various techniques in watercolour painting. The exploration of combined techniques and mixed media will also be considered. Students are encouraged to be bold in experimentation. Assignments, individual critiques and group discussions will be conducted regularly to broaden concepts and methods of expression. Emphasis is on individual approach.

title: Clerical and Regular Scripts
description: This course provides an in-depth study of clerical and regular scripts. Students will be introduced to the various important schools of the two scripts and will have opportunities for practical exercises. Through the study of representative works (including clerical scripts of the Han and Tang dynasties, stele rubbings of the Wei and Tang dynasties), students can master the technique in these scripts and develop their own styles.

title: Mineral-pigment Painting
description: In the history of Chinese art, particularly in the realm of Chinese mural art, the use of mineral pigments as the primary painting medium is now known as mineral-pigment painting. Mineral-pigment painting once had a glorious past, and the Dunhuang murals are still hailed as classic works of art.This course hopes to inherit and protect the precious cultural heritage of mineral-pigment painting, and to expand the use of the aesthetic qualities of mineral pigments, combined with individual creative concepts and expression techniques, to become a unique modern painting medium.As an ancient painting material, mineral pigment has both the heavy-body covering characteristics of oil and the transparency of watercolor, and now is being ‘ rediscovered’ by many contemporary artists ; not only the course will cover traditional method, but will also explore various possibilities in contemporary expression of mineral pigment painting.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: Understand the history of mineral-pigment painting and appreciate the unique beauty of classical Chinese murals; Understand the development of mineral-pigment painting to the present; Understand and master the materials and tools required for mineral-pigment painting; Master the steps and techniques required for mineral-pigment painting; Be aware of the uniqueness and limitations of mineral pigments; Experiment, reconstruct or replace elements of mineral pigment painting and technical process; and Independently complete mineral-pigment paintings and express personal ideas.

title: Becoming a Comics Director
requirements: Pre-requisite: FAAS1100
description: In addition to artistic skills such as drawing, composition and the understanding of color, storytelling is one of the essentials of comics art. These skills in isolation are however not sufficient to create original comics and this art form can only exist through the proper arrangement of visual elements and image-text interactions. This course aims to provide students with the necessary understanding to further develop their understanding of visual and narrative communication through the creation of a story in the form of comics. In order to enhance students’ capacity to create such an interaction of narrative and images, workshops in the assisted creation of stories will be provided alongside the development of the student’s own visual research. Students will also be encouraged to find their own visual language and graphic style. Comic writing is a demanding profession that requires a number of specialized skills. This course will offer training and tutorials in the skills most appropriate to comics creation such as character design, script writing and the kind of sensitive observation that leads to intelligent creativity. Other specialized skills, such as insights into the marketing of comics and management of high-pressure schedules, will also be presented to students; this course will prepare potential comics creators for any future challenge in the profession.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  1. Understand and master comics drawing tools as well as basic digital technical skills 2. Research a comics project through the creation of a sketch book 3. Understand and master character design 4. Understand and master story telling techniques for comics 5. Understand and master the creation of a story board 6. Present their own projects in the form of presentation and the creation of a comics fans page

title: Basic Photography
description: This course covers the basic theories and characteristics of photography, with an aim towards introducing students to the unique visual language of photography through application of photographic equipment, formats and materials. Students will be able to explore and appreciate the nature and culture of photography by learning different photographic approaches through discussions and practice.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  - understand basics of camera and photographic paper; - understand the differences of the analogue and digital format of photographic imaging; - experiment and explore with alternative techniques through darkroom facilities; and  - understand different approaches and esthetics of photography.

Understand styles and artistic approaches of different periods in Western Art History, such as classical period, modern and postmodernism through various exercises; and 4. Develop ability of evaluation through class critique.

title: Mixed Media
description: After World War II, art media are no longer confined to specific materials, tools and techniques. Artists tend to think and make art through idea rather than material. This has caused confusion between conceptual art and visual art. This course will teach students the basic concepts of mixed media, and provide students with a framework for artistic creation, when no well-defined boundaries for material and technique can serve as a reference. Focus will be put on the three principles of mixed media, namely, physicality, cultural signification and spirituality.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to understand: - how to practice contemporary art, such as concept, method and it’s operation in society  - how concept could be elaborated and manifested through material - how to appreciate idea driven art - develop individual skill and approach of mixed media; and - critical thinking in art

title: Art, Archive and Technology
description: This course examines the intersection of contemporary art practices with archives, data analytics, and technology. It delves into the dialectic relations between history, archive, and art. Furthermore, we will explore immersive narratives as a means to showcase contemporary art practices, using archives to investigate the present and envision the future.The course begins with an analysis of seminal theoretical texts and case studies in archival art practices. We will then delve into the fundamental concepts of data analytics, exploring how algorithms and big data have transformed our methods of acquiring knowledge. Students will critically assess the approaches and challenges of artists’ archival practices and data analytics tools through theoretical discussions and case studies of various artworks. These discussions will emphasize how artists engage with data or inventories to interpret and think. Students will complete a creative project to synthesize their learning.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. Identify the seminal theoretical text related to archival practices in contemporary art;2. Reflect on and develop artistic strategies in relation to archiving by understanding critical archival art practices;3. Demonstrate the understanding of algorithm thinking through the basic use of data analytical tools;4. Demonstrate an understanding of the basic use of digital preservation application;5. Demonstrate an understanding of virtual technologies through the basic use of both software and hardware applications; and6. Reflect on how contemporary art concept, data analytics, and technology intersect by creating an immersive narrative work.
syllabus: 1. Introduction: Archival Art Practice in Digital AgeIn this introductory session, we will cover fundamental ideas and debates surrounding archival art practice in contemporary art. How do the digital aspects that challenge traditional archival history reshape our understanding of archival art practice?  To what extent can these challenges be leveraged as opportunities for art practice using digitally enhanced tools within Digital Humanities?This class will also introduce the course structure, reading materials, teaching methods, timetable, and assignments.2. The Archival Impulse and Contemporary ContingenciesThis class will explore the powerful impulse to archive in contemporary culture and its significance in historical knowledge and remembrance. It will also examine the evolving attitudes toward archives in modern and postmodern art, focusing on how artists engage with archival practices and create counter-archives.3. Memory, Forgetting, and Re-presentation in Archival ArtThis class will investigate the role of memory and forgetting in archival art. It will discuss how traces in documents and archives serve as testimony to past events and how artists use these traces to create new narratives. The concept of “détournement” in collage and the practice of collecting will also be explored.4. The Digital Archive and Ephemeral ArtThis class will examine the impact of digital technologies on archival practices, focusing on the transition from physical to digital archives. It will discuss the fluid and dynamic nature of digital archives and their potential for new memory cultures. The class will also explore the ephemeral nature of contemporary archival art and its implications for preservation and memory.5 What is Data Science?This class will cover the fundamental concepts of data science and the latest developments in AI for text analysis, particularly in the context of big data. We will also consider the impact of data on archival practices. Additionally, we will discuss the features and limitations of data mining in cultural analytics.6. Data Science Tools Explore the tools of data science that relate to archival art and the ethical considerations of using AI tools. Discuss the concept of algorithms in text analysis, focusing on the open-source data mining software, which uses a set of rules or procedures to perform various data analysis tasks. Examine the impact of digital technologies on text analysis and data visualization.7. Workshops on Digital Preservation In this class, students will be introduced to the fundamental technologies of virtuality, under the category of Extended Reality (XR) and 3D scanning. We will discuss the unique characteristics of computational media, distinguishing it from other forms of media. And its application on digital preservation.8. Workshops on Virtual RealityThis workshop will teach students the basic use of software and hardware tools to create virtual immersive narratives. Students will gain practical skills for integrating technology into their artistic practices, enhancing their ability to produce digital art experiences with articulation of concepts and methods from the course.

title: Digital Imaging Workshop
description: The course is designed to explore the concepts, aesthetics, and techniques of digital imaging from both academic and studio perspectives. Both technical and aesthetic issues will be addressed. Aesthetic issues encompass concept, composition and historical context, whereas technical topics include raster and vector imaging, image manipulation, time-based 2D graphics, animation and other related topics. Digital imaging software and hardware will also be introduced to illustrate the principles and techniques and to produce the projects.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  -create still 2D compositions exploring visual elements such as points, lines, forms, colors, and symbols, in a digital environment; -create 2D compositions and animations with digitally captured images, computer-generated images and found images with a sense of rhythm and structure; and -present computer-based artwork (image) with appropriate presentation hardware and space, such as projection, screen, monitor, and printing materials.

title: Jades for Life and Death
description: The signature products of the major jade-working centres of the Neolithic period (ca. 5000-2000 BCE), their possible meanings, functions, and implications for cultural exchange as reflected in recent excavations will be the focus of the first half of this course. The subsequent changes in function and meaning, and the development of new forms to accompany these changes, will be examined during the second part of the course, aiming for an understanding of the changing meanings of jade in the ritual, religious, political, and social context of the time. Original works of art from the Art Museum and local collections may be used for instruction when appropriate.

title: Jingdezhen and Beyond: History of Later Chinese Ceramics
description: As the “Capital of Porcelains”, Jingdezhen has played an important role in the history of later Chinese ceramics. This course will examine the organization, the mode of production and the artistic characteristics of the monochrome and painted porcelains of Jingdezhen, to understand the achievements of the Ming and Qing ceramic industry. Trade ceramics and its influence, as well as ceramic production in Hong Kong will also be discussed with a field visit to a ceramic kiln site at Tai Po.

title: Art of the Elite: Calligraphy from Song to Qing
description: This course traces the development of calligraphy from Song to Qing. Major topics include the Song expressive calligraphic styles, Yuan revivalism, model-calligraphy tradition from Ming to mid-Qing, and stele-calligraphy tradition since mid-Qing. In addition to major calligraphers and their masterworks and styles, this course will also examine the philosophical ideas embodied in calligraphy, thus providing students with a cultural understanding of why calligraphy has been regarded as an art of the elite in China.

title: Contemporary Art: Artistic Strategies in a Postmodern Era
description: The goal of this course is to explore Western art and theory from approximately 1945 to the mid-1990s. Special attention will be given to the shift from a modernist to a postmodernist culture, and how artists have endeavoured to address a new era characterized by globalization and consumerism. Whenever possible, contemporary Chinese artworks will be explored for the purposes of cross-cultural comparison.

title: Media Art: Body, Technology, Time
description: This course presents an overview of significant theories and case studies in media art history, spanning from the Enlightenment to the 21st century. It will introduce discourses and histories in Europe, America, and Asia. Topics and mediums discussed include the camera obscura, early film, intermedia installations, Net art, the digital turn, sound art, media art preservation, performance, and digital theatre. Class activities will include a visit to a local museum or archive, group discussions, and a presentation at the end of the semester. Drawing on key artworks and fundamental theories, it aims to guide students to explore how media-based practices evolved in various social environments responding to the history of technology, and develop research skills for academic writing and curating.

title: Buddhist Art and Architecture
description: (UGEC3308 is double-coded with FAAS3110.) This survey explores the historical development of Buddhist visual and material culture from around 5th century BCE to 20th century CE in Asia from a trans-regional perspective. Major topics include, but are not limited to, (1) worship icons, (2) materiality and ritual protocols, (3) iconography and iconometry, (4) illustrations, manuscripts, and pictorial narratives, (5) relics and other charismatic objects, (6) sacred space and monumental architecture, (7) artistic styles and their development and diffusion, and (8) patronage and socio-political context. The course also introduces the religion of Buddhism viewed uniquely in light of archaeological context.

title: Chinese Ceramic Technology: Theory and Practice
description: The aim of this course is to explore the technology of ancient Chinese ceramics through both lectures and workshops. A selection of classic wares from major kilns will be discussed in the lectures. Focuses will be placed on the technique of firing, forming and decorating ceramics and the related kiln technology. Meanwhile students will have opportunities in workshops to apply various ceramic techniques they learn in the lectures to the actual making of ceramics. This course can be taken as either an Art History or a Studio Arts elective course but students are required to declare their choice of attribution in their final year of attendance.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  - understand the history and basic technology of representative Chinese ceramics; - develop skills in writing essay on ceramics; and - apply their knowledge on Chinese ceramic technology in making ceramics.

title: Auspicious Metal: the Ritual Bronzes of Ancient China
description: With special emphasis on recent excavations, this course will look at the artistic and technological development of cast-bronze artifacts from around 1600 BCE to the last few centuries BCE, in an attempt to understand China’s unique achievements in relation to other ancient Bronze Age civilizations. Ritual bronze vessels and weapons will be studied as reflections not only of artistic developments, but also of political, social, religious, and economic developments of the time. Original works of art will be used as teaching material when appropriate.
outcome: After completing the course, student will: - have a firm grasp of the “masterpieces” of ancient China’s bronze-casting tradition from the 2nd millennium B.C. to the beginning of the Christian era, from both archaeological excavations and museum collections worldwide;  - understand the special characteristics of bronze-casting techniques in ancient China and how it developed to meet different needs of the society – as props for state and religious rituals, as functional weapons for battle, as luxury status symbols for the elite etc. ; - appreciate the unique qualities of ancient China’s bronze-casting technology as a reflection not only of artistic sensibilities, but also as reflections of political, social, religious, and economic developments of the time; and - be prepared to pursue in-depth (including graduation-level independent thesis research) some of the key issues related to metal technologies and their artistic, cultural, and economic role in ancient China and/or early societies in general

title: The Art of Chinese Seals
description: This course provides an overview of the artistic characteristics and development of Chinese seals. Content includes the function, forms and related historical issues of ancient seals, and the style and theory of different artistic schools since the Ming and Qing dynasties.

title: Art Under Imperial Patronage: Chinese Court Painting
description: The course traces the development of Chinese court painting since the Han and Tang dynasties with special reference to the Song and the Qing periods. To evaluate the genre objectively in the historical, artistic and cultural perspectives, extant works will be studied side by side with related literature to reveal the content and style of masterpieces in relation to imperial tastes, political implication, cultural heritage, artistic techniques and Western influences.

title: Modern Challenges: Chinese Art of the Twentieth Century
description: This course traces the development of Chinese art during the twentieth century. Major topics to be covered include new directions of traditionalism and westernization for innovation before 1949, as well as the development of Chinese art on the Mainland and elsewhere since 1949. Special attention will be paid to Chinese artists’ artistic response to political turmoil, cultural changes and Western influences in the new era.

title: Western Art II: from Impressionism to the Late 1940s
description: The latter part of the nineteenth century was a time of economic, technological and social change when traditional values were challenged. This revolutionary period marked the beginning of the modern age and the birth of many avant-garde movements. This course aims to examine the various manifestations of these movements and the utopian project they tried to materialize.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - know the general timeframe of the developments of Western art from the late 19th century to the 1960s;  - be able to situate an artwork (sculpture, painting and architecture) within a time period: for example, recognize whether a painting is a Pointillist or a Futurist work; and - understand the historical background of each period and art movement. - be able to think and write like an art historian, a curator and an art critic.

World Art History and the Rise of Western Modernism. London: Phaidon, 2003.  (Additional references will be provided in individual lectures.)

title: Daoist Art
description: This course explores the development of Daoist art, with emphasis on studying artwork in relation to the religious culture and historical context of its production. It concerns how Daoist artwork is linked to Daoist thought, texts and visual culture current in the same period. Students will be introduced to Daoist sculptures, stone carvings, architecture, murals, scripture illustrations, as well as arts that embody Daoist aesthetics and culture, such as landscape paintings, container gardens and garden designs. Through studying archaeological and extant Daoist art and artifacts, together with scholarly research on Daoism and religious art theories, students are expected to acquire in-depth understanding of the development, function and meaning of Daoist art.

title: Western Painting II
description: Emphasis is placed on the development of personal imagery and creative expression. Students will be asked to choose a theme or visual idea for exploration. They are not directed to work in any specific style but are encouraged to use the various concepts and techniques to produce expressive paintings. Frequent class discussions and critiques encourage an exchange of ideas.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:   - understand the materiality and image representation of painting from the perspective of studio art through contemporary art approach; and - develop individual project on painting.
syllabus: Composition and Order Image and Space Transformation and Distortion Expression and Style
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Printmaking
description: Students in this course learn the principles and techniques of intaglio, relief, planography, and serigraphy. Through learning the techniques on drawing, making and copying of print, students could receive fine arts education from the printmaking course. In addition to teaching various materials and making techniques concerning printmaking, this course also discusses related knowledge on presswork, television, computer and mass media, such as the combination and analysis of colours, craftwork on paper making, the disposal of chemical materials, etc. Regular individual tutorials conducted throughout the course provide students with professional guidance enabling them to master the traditional printmaking techniques and also a new approach to aesthetic value.
outcome: After the course, students will be able to  -learn about the off-set printing techniques, wood-cut , stone carving, rubbing, silkscreen in daily and industrial products, and colour reparation -master the traditional printmaking techniques and the new approach to aesthetic value -possess the ability of independent creation
syllabus: Intaglio Relief Planography Serigraphy
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Running and Cursive Scripts
description: This course provides a more focused study in running and cursive scripts and includes both a specialized study of important schools and practical exercises in the two scripts. Students are expected to master running and cursive scripts, in preparation for developing their own styles.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - manage writing methods of running and cursive scripts;  - copy several styles of Chinese calligraphy in running and cursive scripts; and - create their own Chinese calligraphy works in running and cursive scripts

title: Xieyi: Chinese Expressive Painting
description: This course focuses on the techniques of painting in an expressive manner i.e. in the literati tradition of "writing the idea". The techniques and forms of expression such as ink, light colouring, heavy colouring are included. Contents of this course will vary with instructors and students. Offerings with different subtitles can be taken up for credit, up to a maximum of two times.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - master various techniques in brushwork, tone variation and coloring in Chinese expressive painting; - copy typical styles by some important Chinese expressive painters; and  - have their own creation in Chinese expressive painting
syllabus: The topics will include: - exercise of various techniques and formats of expression in Chinese expressive painting including outlining, boneless, ink, light colouring, heavy colouring, medium style and free style; and - study of typical style by some important Chinese expressive painters.
required_readings: 劉紹勇：《筆墨技法詳解》，農村讀物出版社。北京，1994年。  (The required readings will be varied according to the topics and will be distributed during lessons)

title: Sculpting Moulding and Casting
description: This course introduces various perspectives of making sculpture in organic form through direct and indirect methods. Focus will be on understanding and transforming forms in nature as well as forms derived from nature. Technical studio will include hand-building techniques, molding, and casting. Students will learn how to think through three dimensional forms and transforming ideas into tangible objects.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - enhance their skill of 3D design; - understand the history, knowledge and practical theory of molding and casting; and - create a bronze sculpture – from idea and concept development, material and structure analysis, thorough techniques application to build and construction.
syllabus: Duplication: Duplication from one mold in plaster. Mold our Body: Figure molding in fiber glass. From geometry to organism: Abstract sculpture in bronze casting.
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Art in Public Space
description: Art in pubic space became an important subject for those who wanted to reconcile the conflict between individual artistic ideas and the common norms in public space in 21st century. The presumption that artist cannot contribute significantly to public sector is questionable nowadays—there are many experiments being done to show that artistic intervention can somehow arouse the awareness of hidden power and political structure of the society. As a citizen or an artist, art has a role to play in public space.Seeing public space as an arena for artistic expression becomes another focus in contemporary art. Gallery, museum which are supposed to be neutral space in showing art is gradually replaced by space with cultural significances; message in art has been put into specific context for holistic examination. The course will cover various art forms in public space, which include traditionally defined public art, such as sculpture and functional objects in public space. The course will also teach student how to realize an art project through management and negotiation among different stakeholders— the client, the public, the technical consultant and the artist.
outcome: After completing the course, students should be able to: 1) understand various forms of public art and their function 2) understand the infra structure and function of different parties involved  3) understand flow and operation of public art project  4) understand communication and contractual matter
syllabus: 1) art, context and space 2) politics, esthetics and function in public art 3) various forms in public art 4) operation and flow of public art project 5) technical matter—manufacture, legal matter and engagement of the general public 6) individual and group project

title: Experimental Drawing
description: This course will introduce various approaches to drawing so as to broaden students’ technical abilities and provoke awareness of contemporary approaches. Emphasis will be made on five major areas: (1) understanding rhythm and lyrical elements of drawing through figure movement; (2) exploring pictorial composition by studying and recomposing classical works; (3) developing visual vocabulary by exercising free association; (4) drawing as narrative; and (5) drawing as a tool to map spaces and activities.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - re-develop different kind of drawing approach; - develop individual skill and approach of mixed media;  - experimental approach and alternative making; and   - understand the imagination of content and representation of drawing
syllabus: -create drawing tools -apply drawing in different media. -digital manipulation of drawing - drawing & text
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Combined Printmaking
description: Expressions of ideas and concepts in the printmaking studio are used to be the earlier print technologies like relief, intaglio, screen printing and lithography, while technologies like photographic and digital printing in nowadays, enrich the possibility of creating Artwork. Combined printmaking experiments with contemporary combinations of print formats to produce multi-layered explorations of the image, line, colour, marks and visual expression.By understanding the characteristics of traditional and modern printing techniques, and the relation between printmaking materials (paper, ink and plate), students are enabled to expand the possibility of image making by transforming the use of printmaking in their own project.

title: Sculpture: Building and Carving
description: This course will focus on the classic approaches to sculpture: addition and subtraction. Metal and wood will be the major materials used. Through addition, students will be trained to weld metal and join wood to produce large-scale sculpture. Through subtraction, students will be able to define details and inner spaces of sculptures.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - understand various fundamental techniques of wood carving and welding; - further master the usage of power tools; and - explore the possibilities of concept by studying and analysis of various Western and Chinese sculptors
syllabus: Direct metal sculpture: Minimal metal sculpture made by welding. From geometry to organism: Wood sculpture made by wood carving.
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Moving Image Workshop
description: The course is designed to explore the concepts, aesthetics and techniques of moving image in digital format from both academic and studio perspectives. Both technical and aesthetic issues will be addressed. Aesthetic issues encompass concept, relationship of sound and image, video installation and historical context. Technical topics include techniques of cinematography, non-linear editing, scene visualization and other related topics. Non-linear editing and compositing software will be introduced to illustrate the principles and techniques and to produce the projects.

title: Figure Sketching
description: The content of this course includes knowledge of human anatomy, sketching of head and statues and sketching of live model. Through a series of exercises, students will acquire a better understanding of depicting human forms. It also enhances students’ powers of expression in figure drawing. The course helps to build the foundation of figure painting which applies for different media.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - understand fundamental knowledge of the human anatomy; - grasp image feature and structure of figure accurately; - improve their ability of observation, understanding and sensibility; and - develop their skill to express themselves in figure painting.
syllabus: This course is designed for students who are interested to learn figure drawing. The course covers fundamental knowledge of the human anatomy for artistic purpose, introduction of the drawing of the masters, sketching exercises from life of heads, features, faces and the draped figure.
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Calligraphy in Ancient Scripts
description: This course aims to provide a more focused study of ancient Chinese calligraphy before the Qin and Han dynasties. In addition to the training of writing skills, the knowledge of paleography will also be introduced. The course lays a foundation for further pursuit of creation and study. This course can be taken as either an Art History or a Studio Arts elective course but students are required to declare their choice of attribution in their final year of attendance.
outcome: This course aims to provide a more focused study in ancient Chinese calligraphy before Qin and Han dynasties. In addition to the training of writing skills, the knowledge of paleography will also be introduced in the course. The design of the course is a foundation for further pursuit of creation and study. It is through the study of Chinese calligraphy in ancient scripts that students can understand the relationship of art and the culture of ancient Chinese society, and can widen their horizon in calligraphy creation, setting a foundation for their study of ancient Chinese art in future.
syllabus: The topics will include: - introduction to ancient Chinese Calligraphy; - writing skills in ancient Chinese Calligraphy including oracle-bone inscription, bronze inscription, stone engravings, bamboo and wooden strips inscription before Qin and Han dynasties; and - knowledge of paleography.

title: Gongbi: Chinese Delineative Painting
description: This is an advanced study of Chinese Painting. It focuses on studying the techniques of painting by using fine-line and wash, one of two primary painting techniques in the Chinese tradition. Technique and forms of expression such as ink, light colouring, heavy colouring are included. Students will be encouraged to initiate artistic creation by incorporating different forms of expression. Contents of this course will vary with instructors and students. Offerings with different subtitles can be taken up for credit, up to a maximum of two times.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: - have a thorough understanding of techniques and forms of expression of Chinese delineative painting; - be able to master the techniques; and - possess the ability of independent creation
syllabus: The topics will include: - introduction to materials and tools used in Chinese delineative painting; - exercise of techniques in brushwork, tone variation and colouring; and - study of typical style by some important Chinese expressive painters.

title: Text and Image
description: To explore the relationship between Text and Image, there are three parts in the course’s content: Creative Writing, Image Making and Critic Writing. Creative Writing includes narrative writing, fictional story, life memories, poetry, stream of consciousness… …etc that given a board based understanding of text. Image Making requires to re-think the application of imagery through representation and interpretation of text that be able to re-generate different images relatively. After the transformation from text to image, through the on-looker’s view point to create Critic Writing that using a third party’s perspective to analysis and re-read different kind of possibilities in the process of art making.

title: Chinese Landscape Painting
description: This course includes introduction of different tools and landscape painting skills. The main learning methods are imitation and copy. It aims to allow students get familiar with traditional painting methods and combine with outdoor sketches to finally have a complete understanding in Chinese landscape painting. The students are expected to be able to integrate what he/she has learned, so as to develop a personal painting style finally.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to: 1. master various techniques in brushwork, tone variation and coloring in Chinese landscape painting; 2. copy typical styles by some important Chinese landscape painters; and  3. have their own creation in Chinese landscape painting
syllabus: - exercise of various techniques and formats of expression in Chinese landscape painting including Tree method, Mountain and stone method, Cloud and water method ,Landscape decorated method, Composition, Landscape in different time, Color arrangementaint , Paint from life ; and - study of typical style by some important Chinese landscape painters.

title: Ceramic Art: Form and Space
description: The course introduces construction skills and knowledge in ceramics through studio practice. Focus will be placed on the creation of form using clay and methods in ceramics. Discussions and critiques will be arranged to enhance the awareness of ceramics in the context of visual culture and contemporary life. Students are encouraged to apply the skills and knowledge learnt in developing their own area of work.
outcome: After completing this course, students will be able to 1. acquire construction skills and knowledge in the area of ceramics; 2. practically construct forms with clay by using different methods; 3. transfer such skills and knowledge in the development of their own area of work; and 4. develop critical dialogue of ceramics in the context of visual culture and contemporary life.
syllabus: The topics will include: 1. Health and safety in ceramic studios 2. Knowledge of material process in clay 3. Hand-building methods and their variations 4. Investigating notions of space through ceramic works 5. Interaction between form and space 6. Perceiving and creating three dimensional forms in contemporary life

description: The course introduces skills and knowledge of creating surfaces on ceramic works. Focus will be placed on exploring and investigating various notions of surface creation in ceramics. Different colouring agents and textures will be applied through traditional and contemporary methods. Through practice and discussion, students are encouraged to explore the role of surfaces on forms in various aspects of contemporary art.

title: Art and Social Engagement: Summer Internship
description: How to engage society through artistic and creative strategies? This course is designed to respond to this question with hands-on experience. This course provides internship placements for students to work with organizations involved in social engagement through creative thinking. Designed in an inter-disciplinary approach, students will not only work closely with artists, but also with social workers, entrepreneurs, designers, therapists, architects, etc. Besides art-administrative works, students are expected to create art projects and assist the organizations in running creative projects during the placement period. Through practical works, students are expected to build capacity to conduct socially-engaged projects in their own in future.Period of placement usually starts from June to August. All interested students must attend the briefing session conducted in February/March.This course can be taken as either an Art History or a Studio Arts elective course but students are required to declare their choice of attribution in their final year of attendance.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  1. Understand how organizations (commercial or non-profit) tackle social issues in creative ways; 2. Enhance their specialty in arts by applying their skills in an institutional and social setting; 3. Know how to deal with obstacles through problem-solving skills; 4. Learn communication skills with professionals in different fields; 5. Build network with institutions and individuals who share similar interests and beliefs; 6. Develop creative skills in implementing social engagement projects using artistic strategies. 7. Understand how public engagement with art can be analyzed and applied in different contexts, in both non-profit and commercial settings; 8. To expand their understanding of social engagement with art in an inter-disciplinary way; 9. To reflect the role of art in contemporary society and how it can be brought to the public.
syllabus: For Undergraduate students year 2 or above, year 3 prioritized. Internship usually starts from June to August. Approximately 150 working hours in 8-10 weeks in total.   Internship Briefing Session in February or March  Matching and interviews with partner institutions in March and April   Internship placement in the agreed period at respective partner institutions  End-of-placement presentation in October or November

title: Tradition and Transformation: Chinese Literati Painting
description: The course traces the development of Chinese literati painting from the Northern Song to the first half of the 20th century. Topics to cover include literati art theories, revivalism, the theory of the Southern and Northern Schools, period styles, regional styles, Ming and Qing schools, reverence for and transformation of antiquity, commercialization of painting, and the modernization of traditional painting.

title: Understanding Theories of Chinese Painting and Calligraphy
description: This course introduces students to the theories of Chinese painting and calligraphy from the Six Dynasties period through the twentieth century. Major theoretical writings will be discussed and analysed to provide students with an understanding of the criteria, views, documentation, principles, and debates of traditional painting and calligraphy. Extant works of painting and calligraphy will be also used as examples to discuss the application of theories.

title: An Illustrated History of Western Art Theory: from Plato to Postmodernism
description: This course is a presentation of the history of Western thought in relation with the visual arts, from Plato to contemporary thinkers (such as Jacques Derrida and Jean-François Lyotard). The works of the most important thinkers will be presented using texts and visual documentation.

title: Art As Profession
description: This course provides students with information and training in preparation for careers as art professionals. Emphasis will be placed on how the art producer, art mediator and the general public interact with each other. Topics will include cultural policies in Hong Kong, the role of the public and private sectors, art in public spaces, art criticism, curatorship, organizing portfolios, exhibitions, and legal issues. In addition, guest speakers will speak on their experiences as art professionals in Hong Kong. This course can be taken as either an Art History or a Studio Arts elective course but students are required to declare their choice of attribution in their final year of attendance.
outcome: After completing this course, students will be able to :  -understand the ecology (education, creation, promotion, conservation, creative cultural industries, cultural entrepreneurship) for art development of Hong Kong and its ultimate goals for development quality life and civil society; -understand the significance of different roles (artist, curator, administrator, critics, educationist, researchers, promoters, audience) in helping to shape the art ecology;  -understand the nature of art organizations/government/corporates/creative industries and their importance in helping to support the development of the art ecology; and  -see the possibilities for themselves career-wise and for contributing to art development within and without Hong Kong.
syllabus: Artist entities and their environment Artist entities and the public sector Artist entities and the private sector How to prepare one to become an art-related professional
required_readings: As it is a studio course, no specific reading is required; the teacher will provide reference and reading material to students from time to time.

title: Seal Carving
description: The advanced course in Chinese arts creation includes an introduction to the materials, tools and techniques of seal carving, and the imprinting and rubbing of seals. Through the analysis and study of representative examples over the centuries, as well as the art of modern seal carving, students can master the different script-forms in seal carving and a wide-range of carving techniques, toward creating their own styles in seal carving. Students are advised to take FAAS3223 before taking this course.
outcome: After completing this course, students will be able to:  - have a thorough understanding of the history and theory of seal carving;  - possess the ability of independent creation; and - develop personal styles
syllabus: The topics will include: - introduction to materials and tools; - exercise of techniques in carving and seal stamping, as well as carving and rubbing the side colophon; and - studies of various masterpieces styles of different dynasties.

title: Creative Workshop I
description: This course is an advance studio course designed for students who have in-depth art experience. The course will teach students methodology of art creation in contemporary era and encourage deal with individual issues on art creation through discussion. Course content includes topics such as the latest development of contemporary art, semiotics and art, revisiting previous works of students, develop new techniques and direction for individual creation. The form of teaching in this course will be lectures, seminars and critiques.

description: This course provides Majors in creative art with guidance in individual research for their graduation project. A series of lectures on art criticism and exegesis writing will prepare students to use their knowledge of art history, art theory and general education to write about their own works and the works of others. Compulsory visits to local art exhibitions will be organized and students will have to submit a mid-term paper in the form of art criticism. As the course is also based on individual supervision, students are also required to plan their graduation thesis and meet their supervisors regularly. At the end of the term, students must submit evidence of their research progress as designated by relevant supervisor(s). Advisory: For final year Majors only.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  - identify their research direction, and provide guidance on conceptual development; - monitor their progress of research and polish their concepts; - understand their strength and weakness, thus to develop necessary skill to cope with their objectives in their graduation work; and - polish their presentation skills, in order to achieve a better result despite various constrains.

title: Theories of Chinese Painting and Calligraphy
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art or Master of Fine Arts
description: This course examines in detail the theories of Chinese painting and calligraphy. Major theoretical works will be discussed and analysed to provide students with an understanding of the criteria, views, documentation, and principles of traditional painting and calligraphy. Twentieth-century theories and their associated debates will also be discussed.

title: Study of Later Chinese Ceramics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art or Master of Fine Arts
description: This course aims to provide a more focused study in the history of Chinese ceramics from the Yuan to the Qing dynasty. It examines the organization, modes of production and artistic characteristics of the imperial porcelains of Jingdezhen, and discusses the interaction between the ceramic industry of Jingdezhen and other production sites inside and outside China. Major research methodologies and approaches to Chinese ceramics will also be introduced. Students are expected to acquire in-depth understanding of the historical development and technological achievements of later Chinese ceramics through studying historical archives, archaeological reports, ceramic samples and scholarly research. They are also required to undertake independent research on selected topics and present a long essay at the end of the course.

title: Schools of Model-calligraphy and Stele Studies
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art or Master of Fine Arts
description: The course aims at tracing the development of Chinese calligraphy from the migration of the model-calligraphy school to the stele school with special reference to the impact of the Jin-Tang tradition on calligraphers down the ages, factors leading to the rise of stele studies in the Qing dynasty, and the issue of transformation on the basis of the great calligraphic traditions. Topics to be covered include calligraphic theories since the Song dynasty, the prevalence of the Model-calligraphies from the Chunhua Archive and other calligraphic carvings, the preference for copying from ancient masters, the relationship between evidential research and calligraphy, and the works and styles of leading masters. Students of the course are required to conduct thematic research and submit an essay at the end of the term.

title: Art in Europe and North America After WWII
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art or Master of Fine Arts
description: The art practices developed after WWII in Europe and North America have differed so profoundly from those preceding it that many art historians have recognized an irreconcilable break between the two periods. Generally referred to as ‘postmodern art,’ still the most convenient way to separate these practices from the ones called ‘modernist,’ it has offered an extraordinarily wide array of media and strategies. This course will explore some of the many choices made by the artists of these two geographical areas by analyzing their art against their cultural and social backgrounds.

title: Daoist Art and Relics
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art, Master of Fine Arts, MA Chinese Art History
description: This course is designed to enhance student's ability to conduct research on religious art. In addition to various Daoist art topics, such as Daoist paintings and sculptures, different research methodologies approaches to Daoist art will be introduced. Students are expected to acquire in-depth understanding of the development, function and meaning of Daoist art through studying archaeological and extant Daoist art and artifacts, together with scholarly research on Daoism and religious art theories. They are also required to undertake independent research on selected Daoist art topics and present a long essay at the end of the course.

title: Special Topics in Art History
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art, Master of Fine Arts, MA Chinese Art History
description: This course examines in detail selected topics in art history, such as case study of archaeological discoveries, art of a dynasty, individual artists, etc. It aims at providing students with a full understanding of certain special areas in the history of art. title: History of Chinese Literati Painting
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art, Master of Fine Arts, MA Fine Arts, MA Chinese Art History
description: The course aims at tracing the development of literati painting with special reference to literati views on painting held by Su Shi and others since the Song dynasty, the styles and influences of leading painters, and the issue of transformation on the basis of the great painting traditions. Topics to be covered include theories of literati painting, personal styles and regional painting schools, perpetuation and reinvention of the traditions, paintings as commodities, and elitist and popular tastes. Students of the course are required to conduct thematic research and submit an essay at the end of the term.
outcome: After completing this course, students will be able to  - analyze the visual features as well as the philosophical, aesthetic and cultural significance of Chinese literati painting;  - evaluate critically the validity of different arguments concerning a work of Chinese literati painting;  - make use of different research approaches and methodologies in conducting independent research; and - write academic papers on Chinese literati painting.

title: Comparative Analysis of 17th and 18th Century Painting
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art or Master of Fine Arts
description: The comparison of theoretical texts written by Chinese and European painters in the 17th and 18th centuries should clarify the differences – and some similarities – present in two artistic traditions that have developed along very different lines. The first part of the course is dedicated to the study and contextualization of representative texts of the period while, in the second part, a number of the comparative themes thus unveiled will be explored in details using also sources other than the domain of visual arts. Although the emphasis of this course will be on the arts of the 17th and 18th centuries, many of the problems raised during this comparative analysis will lead to an exploration of some issues concerning contemporary art in China and the rest of the world.

title: Art Theory in Europe and North America From Antiquity to the Present
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art or Master of Fine Arts
description: Even a cursory knowledge of Euro-American contemporary art will lead to the realization that one needs to know the writings to understand the visual. If the present situation seems to have made the existence of theory in texts necessary, art theory has however existed for a very long time and in many different forms. To better understand the often very complex thinking that accompanies present-day art practices, it is necessary to understand the history of the thought attached to art. This course specializes in the thinking about art made in Europe and North America from the Antiquity to the present. Three kinds of texts will therefore be used: the writings produced by philosophers about aesthetics and art; the art theory and art criticism written in the public sphere; as well as the writings made by artists on their own practices.

title: History of Chinese Court Painting
requirements: For students in MPhil-PhD Chinese Art, Master of Fine Arts, MA Fine Arts, MA Chinese Art History
description: This course traces the development of Chinese court painting from the Qin dynasty through the Qing dynasty. Each class will examine the production and transmission of court painting in light of key concepts in the discourse of Chinese art, which include but are not limited to: stylistic and technical features, political implication, imperial painting academy, genres in art, art patronage, and cross-cultural interactions.

title: Media Art History
requirements: For students in Master of Fine Arts, MPhil-PhD Chinese Art
description: What are the intersections between art and technology? Have artists always been optimistic about analogue and digital media? This seminar presents major theories and case studies within media art history, extending from the Enlightenment to the 21st century. The first part of the course offers a summary of technological progress in optical and sound media, together with their resurgence within the modern art world. It further supplies theoretical models for examining the aesthetics of moving image art, especially regarding temporality and performativity. The second part concentrates on the evolution of time-based media art across Asia. The topics and mediums covered encompass the camera obscura, early film, intermedia installations, Net art, the digital shift, sound art, media art conservation, performance, and digital theatre. Course activities encompass a trip to a nearby museum or archive, group discussions, and a presentation. Relying on essential artworks and core theories, it seeks to direct students in examining how media-based practices developed within diverse social contexts in reaction to technological history, while cultivating research abilities for scholarly writing and curating.
