title: Contemporary Art
requirements: For students in MA Fine Arts
description: The goal of this course is to explore Western art from approximately 1945 to the mid- 1990s and especially the shift from a modernist to a postmodern culture, as well as how artists have endeavored to address a new era characterized by globalization and consumerism. In parallel, this course will also trace the development of Chinese art during the 20th century. Special attention will be paid to Chinese artists’ response to the political turmoil and cultural changes of the last fifty years.
outcome: After completing this course, students will be able to: - understand the general timeframe of the developments of Chinese and Western art from the 1960s to the present days; - understand the social and artistic background of the works of a large number of contemporary artists in order to make them aware of the latest developments in the art field as well as help them find meaning in their own art practices; and - create an informed opinion on any artwork produced in the postmodern period.

title: Chinese Art
requirements: For students in MA Fine Arts
description: This course aims at providing students with a foundation of Chinese art history which serves as a key source of reference for their artistic creation. Through studying masterpieces of different Chinese artistic traditions, such as painting, calligraphy, religious sculpture, ceramics, lacquer, students will understand the special characteristic and historical development of pre-20th century Chinese art. Special attention will be given to changes in concepts, ways of expression, art techniques and cultural significance of each artistic tradition. Students will be required to conduct thematic research and submit an essay at the end of the term.

description: This course is designed to timely address special issues in visual arts, to provide students with opportunities for in-depth studies with specialists/teachers familiar with current art practices that are normally not covered by our undergraduate curriculum. title: Creative Workshop
requirements: For students in MA Fine Arts
description: This course is designed to help students refine their skills and consolidate their knowledge in artistic creation. description: In this course, the production and consumption of culture will be considered with reference to discourses of culture industry and creative economy among other things. title: Chinese Painting and Calligraphy of the Twentieth Century
requirements: For students in MA Fine Arts, MA Chinese Art History
description: This course traces the development of Chinese Painting and calligraphy in the twentieth century. Major topics to be covered include the influence of foreign styles on Chinese painting and the localization of oil painting in the early twentieth century, the impact of politics on Chinese art making since 1949, as well as the new waves after the reform and opening-up of China, exploring in depth the ways of reform and modernization of Chinese painting and calligraphy in the new era. Through the studies on major Chinese artists and their representative works, the course will provide insights into how the political, economic and social changes, different artistic environments, confrontation and exchange of Chinese and foreign cultures affect the artistic creations and ideas of Chinese painters and calligraphers in the past century.

title: Chinese Art History
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course aims to provide foundational knowledge of Chinese art history from the Neolithic period to the Qing Dynasty. It introduces to students major artistic traditions of China, such as pottery, jade, bronze, porcelain, and painting. Their material properties, production techniques, developments, masterpieces and their producers, key research topics and methods will be discussed. Through essay reading, class presentation and discussion, and academic paper writing, this course will enhance students’ academic research abilities and lay a comprehensive foundation for further in-depth research on various materials and topics in Chinese art history.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. have a good understanding of major artistic traditions of China, such as pottery, jade, bronze, porcelain, and painting;2. identify the material properties, production techniques, masterpieces and their producers, key research topics and methods of major artistic traditions;3. analyze academic articles and arguments of Chinese art history;4. present Chinese works of art and their historical significance academically;5. write academic essays on topics of Chinese art history.
syllabus: 1.    Pottery (I)Materials and production techniques: clay, glaze and kiln firing. Overview of Neolithic pottery traditions from 6000BCE to 2000BCE. Form and decoration of potteries in relation to different Neolithic settlements. 2.    Pottery (II)Material and technological development: white pottery, proto-porcelain and lead glaze. Overview of pottery development from 2000BCE to 907CE. Pottery vessels, funeral figurines and models, and the contexts of their use. 3.    Jade (I)Material properties and distribution of Jade and Jadeite. title: Modern and Contemporary Asian Art
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: The course examines the defining moments in the development of modern and contemporary art, primarily in East Asia, with selected topics from South-Asia or South-East Asia as points of comparison. Anchored by a significant movement or trend, each session focuses on the relationship between selected artistic events and the social, political, cultural, and technological conditions of its emergence. A wide range of media, from painting, sculpture, and print-making to photography, video, installation, and performance art, will be considered. Situating the key aesthetic transformations that defined art’s modernity and contemporary transformations in a broader historical context, the course explores art historical discourses and approaches that have been developed very recently, with an aim to forge an analysis of an emerging subject. Their relationship to the rise of global art discourses about non-Western art as well as its cross-sections with modern and contemporary art in Europe and North America will be heeded. Students will examine the tempus and locus of the modern and contemporary, as well as the social and cultural conditions of their developments, and the important works and “texts” that constitute the global contemporary.The case studies in this course offer a testing ground to think about new approaches to writing art histories and displaying contemporary art. The following questions will be explored: How is “modern,” “contemporary” and “avant-garde” in China, Japan, and India different from their European counterparts? What are the moments that constitute “modernity” and “contemporaneity” in Asian art? Are “styles,” “isms” and “movements” appropriate criteria to judge modern and contemporary Asian Art? What would be other ways to contextualize these global trends?
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. Identify and critique key research methods employed in modern and contemporary Asian art;2. Use the comparative approach to analyse key debates, aesthetic criteria, and cultural differences in modern and contemporary Asian art;3. Differentiate and explain advanced theoretical frameworks relevant to the field of global contemporary art;4. Apply theoretical frameworks and methods relevant to Asian modern and contemporary art in research papers and advanced projects such as curation and exhibition catalogues.
syllabus: Introduction: From Modernism to Modernisms and ContemporaneityThis introductory session provides an overview on the emergence and dynamics of Modern art movements in Asia. We will discuss selected art historical papers on East Asian Modernism and contemporaneity, particularly in China and Japan.Colonialism and Cultural TransmissionsThis session is devoted to the history of cultural interchange between Asia and Europe since the late 19th Century. We will explore the system of arts education and institution in early modernism, as well as the issue of transmission of style.Modern Art in JapanThis session deals with Modern art in Japan and is divided into three subtopics: Yoga, Nihonga, and Calligraphic abstraction. The construction of these concepts, the hybridity of styles, as well as their transcultural historical backgrounds will be tackled.Critique of Euroamerican Modernism: Japan and KoreaTwo sessions will be devoted to three art “schools” or “movements” in East Asia, namely Monoha, Tansaekhwa, and Gutai which consciously responded to Eurocamerican modern art. We will compare and analyse their diverse strategies of gestural abstraction and environmentalism.Modern Art in IndiaOne session will provide an overview of Indian modernism until the 1970s, from academic Realism, Abstraction, to pop art. Modern Art in the Chinese Speaking WorldTwo sessions will be devoted to various “schools” of Realism and Abstraction in China from the early 20th century to the 1960s.Identity, Cultural Representation, and the Biennale Effect post-1980sTwo sessions will be devoted to the turn to the global contemporary. Topics we will discuss include New Wave Art in China, Indian Art since the 1980s, the biennale effect, as well art exchange within Asia-Pacific.Activism and Performance in Contemporary Asian Art   Two sessions will be devoted to avant-garde, body art, and intermedia in Japan, China, and Indonesia. Gender Perspectives and Women ArtistsThis session provides an overview on images of women, women artists and feminist criticisms since modernism.

title: Painting in East Asia
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: China, Japan, and Korea each have a long and rich painting history, yet the works from these three countries share common elements in format, theme, technique, and theory. Since the Tang and Song dynasties, the ruling classes, scholars, monks, collectors, and painters across East Asia have been familiar with and have highly valued paintings from neighboring regions. Therefore, this course will not only introduce the representative paintings and their artistic styles from the three countries and the social, cultural, religious, political, and economic contexts that shaped their unique expressions and distributions, but will also explore how cross-border interactions, both public and private, contributed to the formation of a distinct East Asian art world.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. identify the distinctive features of paintings from China, Japan, and Korea and the historical contexts that shaped these artworks;2. examine the impact of cross-border interactions on the evolution of painting styles, themes, techniques, and theories across East Asia;3. assess the contributions of various social groups, including the imperial and royal courts, scholars, monks, and collectors, to the patronage, circulation, and preservation of paintings in China, Japan, and Korea;4. recognize the uniqueness of the East Asian artistic network.
syllabus: 1.    The Origin and Development of Chinese Painting: To explore what defines Chinese painting as distinctly Chinese.2.    The Origin and Development of Japanese Painting: To explore what defines Japanese painting as distinctly Japanese.3.    The Origin and Development of Korean Painting: To explore what defines Korean painting as distinctly Korean.4.    Eight Views Painting in East Asia: To introduce the literary and political backgrounds of the Eight Views paintings popular in China, Japan, and Korea, as well as the different artistic expressions of this theme in each country.5.    Chinese Paintings in Japanese Collections (I) Ningbo Buddhist Painting: To introduce the commission and artistic features of Ningbo Buddhist paintings, and their transmission to Japan.6.    Chinese Paintings in Japanese Collections (II) Kundaikan sayū chōki: To introduce the different connoisseurship of painting between China and Japan through examining Chinese paintings from the shogun’s collection and Japanese documents.7.    Goryeo Buddhist Painting: To introduce the visual features of extant Goryeo Buddhist paintings and their transmission in Korea, Japan, and beyond.8.    Ink Painting in East Asia: To explore the origins and differences between Chinese and Japanese ink painting.9.    Zhe School Painting in East Asia: To explain the definition of the “Zhe School” and this painting style’s popularity and decline in China, Japan, and Korea.10.    Literati Painting in East Asia: To assess the origin of the painting theory of the “Southern and Northern Schools” and the varying expressions and adoption by painters from various social classes of the Chinese literati painting style in different countries.

title: Chinese Ceramics in Global Contexts
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course traces the development of Chinese ceramics in local and global contexts from the 16th to the 19th century. It explores Ming and Qing China and its exchanges and mutual learning with the world’s civilizations in the field of ceramics. Major topics include the economic and social background of the Ming and Qing dynasties and the development of the ceramics industry, the opening of direct sea routes between China and the world and the global circulation of Chinese ceramics, the exchange of culture, art, science, and technology using ceramics as a medium, the spread of Chinese ceramics to the West and the key role it played in the rise of the European porcelain industry. Through studies of objects, combined with Chinese and Western documentary records and historical images, the course will reconstruct the development of Chinese ceramics and its unique craft and cultural achievements in the globalization matrix, and provide insights into the unique role of Chinese ceramics in the development of world ceramics.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. have a basic understanding of the development of Chinese ceramics and its unique craft and cultural achievements in the 16th to 19th centuries;2. know some of the most important examples that show the encounter and exchange of culture, art, science and technology between China and the world using ceramics as a medium;3. identify some of the most famous pieces of ceramics produced in China and their target markets;4. recognise some of the most iconic elements from the themes, patterns and forms of ceramic pieces and gain a general idea of their cultural origins;5. form a scholarly opinion on global fashion trends in ceramic art during the 16th to 19th centuries and their relationship to political and historical events;6. develop skills in handling objects, interpreting exhibitions, writing academic essays and presenting to the public.

Yixing in Jiangsu Province; and Zhangzhou and Dehua in Fujian Province.Manufacture and Transport of Porcelain: Historical Documents and Export Paintings- Documents showing that the European missionaries, explorers and merchants who lived in China had been trying to make secret enquiries or records about porcelain since the late Ming period.- As a special type of export commodity, some of the export paintings of Canton illustrate the manufacture, transport and sale of export porcelain.Braving the Ocean Waves I: The Global Transport of Chinese Ceramics- The main routes of merchant ships from the 16th to the 19th century.- The major countries and companies that controlled the trading ports and sailing routes.Braving the Ocean Waves II: Shipwrecks and their Ceramic Cargoes- Famous shipwrecks from the 16th to 19th centuries.- Underwater archaeology and the ceramic treasures discovered and salvaged from deep sea.Fashion of All Nations I: Chinese Ceramics in Asia and the New World of the Americas- Chinese ceramics in Japan: tea ceremony, flower ceremony, and Kaiseki-ryōri.- Chinese ceramics in Southeast Asia and the Middle East: daily objects, rural artefacts and indicators of family wealth.- Chinese ceramics in the New World of the Americas: porcelain currency.Fashion of All Nations II: Chinese Ceramics in Europe- Chinese porcelain wares and the daily life and artistic tastes of European royals and aristocrats; chinoiserie; fashion for porcelain table services, and porcelain sets for tea, coffee, and chocolate drinking.- Chinaware copying the shapes of Western glassware and metalware; decorative themes derived from Western myths, biblical stories and coats of arms; the export and popularity of Imari porcelain.- Porcelain wares made in Jingdezhen and decorated in European workshops.- The explorations of European artists, scientists and potters in search of the secrets of Chinese porcelain.Profound Impact of Chinaware II: The Rise of the European Porcelain Manufactory- Augustus II the Strong and his passion for Chinese porcelain; the first European hard-paste porcelain created in Meissen.- Royal Delft and the efforts of the Dutch to copy Chinese blue-and-white.- The unique role that Chinese porcelain played in the rise of the European porcelain manufactory from the 18th century onwards.

title: Chinese Art Display and Communication
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course explores the ways in which knowledge and concepts of Chinese art and antiquities are conveyed to contemporary audiences through public display. A range of contexts in which Chinese art and antiquities are curated will be discussed, from the display of actual art objects in public and private museums, commercial galleries, and auction houses, to the use of digital media to showcase Chinese art and antiquities in virtual and physical museums. Students will be equipped with basic theories of art curation and communication, exposed to different settings of art display, engaged in dialogues with curators, and encouraged to reflect on various strategies of Chinese art curation through case studies. Site visits will be arranged to provide students with firsthand experience of different types of art display and their effectiveness in communicating with the audience. Museum curators and art specialists will be invited to share their curatorial concepts and experiences.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. understand the basic theories of art curation and communication;2. identify the different backgrounds and characteristics of public and private museums, commercial galleries, auction houses, and virtual museums where Chinese art and antiquities are curated;3. critically examine curatorial concepts behind the display of Chinese art and antiquities; 4. reflect on various strategies for conveying knowledge and concepts of Chinese art and antiquities to contemporary audience.
syllabus: 1. Introduction to Chinese Art Collection and Display How did Chinese art and antiquities become collectibles worldwide from the 19th century, leading to the establishment of major museums and collections where the majority of public displays of Chinese art and antiquities take place nowadays?2. Display of Art and Antiquities in Public and Private Museums What are the core characteristics and features of public and private museums? Why is curation important in the display of art and antiquities?3. Case Study I: Chinese Art Exhibition in Museums What are the factors that contribute to a “successful” exhibition of Chinese art? How does the display of art objects shape our understanding of the objects and its related history?An ongoing exhibition will be chosen as the subject of discussion with site visit followed by class discussion.4. Case Study II: Chinese Art Exhibition in Museums How does the combination of art object display, virtual exhibition tours, and publication of exhibition catalogues influence the viewer's perception of the featured art objects and the curatorial concepts of the exhibition?An exhibition will be chosen as the subject of discussion.5. In Dialogue with Curators How do museum curators convey curatorial concepts through art objects? What are the factors that influence the curatorial direction, selection, and interpretation of exhibits, as well as the presentation strategies of an exhibition? How should an exhibition be assessed, and how can visitor reactions be gauged?A museum curator will be invited to share with students.6. Display of Art and Antiquities in Commercial Spaces What are the characteristics and features of commercial spaces as venues for art display?7. Site VisitWhat strategies are employed to create meaning and value for Chinese art and antiquities displayed in various commercial venues?Guided tour will be arranged to visit commercial galleries or auction houses. 8. In Dialogue with Auction House SpecialistsHow is value created through the display and cataloguing of art objects?An auction house or gallery specialist will be invited to share with students.9. Digital Technology in Art DisplayWhat kinds of digital technology are involved in the display of Chinese art and antiquities in museums?10. Curation through Digital MediaHow does cultural understanding and interpretation reach audiences through the display of art objects and monuments via digital media? How do audiences react to this alternative form of art display?11. Case StudyHow far can curatorial concepts and knowledge of Chinese art be conveyed through digital media to audiences in comparison with the display of physical art objects?Past or present examples of using the technology of Virtual Reality (VR) or Augmented Reality (AR) to disseminate knowledge and concepts of Chinese art and antiquities will be selected for discussion.

title: Chinese Calligraphy: Theory, Masterpieces and Connoisseurship
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course traces the development of Chinese calligraphy from pre-Qin periods to the twentieth century. In addition to calligraphic theories, scripts, major calligraphers and their masterworks and styles, this course will also examine the philosophical ideas embodied in calligraphy, thus providing students with a better understanding of the historical development, cultural meaning, legacy, and connoisseurship in Chinese calligraphy.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. understand the whole development of the Chinese calligraphy from the pre-Qin periods to the twentieth century;2. recognize key calligraphic masterpieces; 3. analyze the visual features as well as the aesthetic, social and cultural significance of Chinese calligraphy;4. evaluate critically the validity of different arguments concerning a work of Chinese calligraphy; and5. write academic papers on Chinese calligraphy.
syllabus: 1. Calligraphy of the pre-Qin periods and the Han dynasty-An introduction of Chinese calligraphy, its script development and use in daily life.-Transformation of oracle bone inscription, bronze inscription, seal script and clerical script.2. Calligraphy of the Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern dynasties -Transformation of cursive, running, and regular scripts.-The Two Wangs traditions, as well as stele carving in the period.3. Calligraphy of the Sui, Tang and Five dynasties-Regular and cursive scripts.-Calligraphy masters and their theories of the Tang dynasty.4. Calligraphy of the Northern Song dynasty-Su Shi, Wang Tingjian, Mi Fu and the Song expressive calligraphic styles.-Model calligraphies from the Chunhua era (Chunhua ge tie).5. Calligraphy of the Southern Song dynasty-The classical calligraphic style in the imperial court.-Rubbings of stone engraving and model calligraphies.6. Calligraphy of the Yuan dynasty-Zhao Mengfu and the revivalism of Yuan calligraphy.7. Calligraphy of the Ming dynasty-Wen Zhengming and the Wu School of calligraphy.-Dong Qichang and the Huating School of calligraphy.8. Calligraphy of the Qing dynasty I-Model calligraphies and the Two Wangs tradition in the early and middle Qing.9. Calligraphy of the Qing dynasty II-The stele school of calligraphy in the late Qing, its theory and innovation.10. Calligraphy of the twentieth century-Different inspirations, schools and characteristics.-Challenges of calligraphy in a new era.11. Hong Kong calligraphy-The continuity of calligraphic tradition in Hong Kong.-Calligraphy, and cultural preservation and daily life in Hong Kong.12. Case study I-The debate of Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Gathering (Lanting xu)13. Case study II-The debate of Monk Huai Su’s Autobiography (Zixu tie).

title: Buddhist Art and Material Culture
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course is designed to enhance student’s ability to conduct research on Buddhist visual and material culture from around 5th century BCE to 20th century CE. It approaches the subject from a trans-Asiatic perspective and introduces to students different research methods. Major topics include (1) worship icons, (2) iconography and iconometry, (3) manuscripts and pictorial narratives, (4) śarīra and other charismatic objects, (5) ritual space and sacred architecture, (6) artistic styles and conventions, and (7) patronage and socio-political context. Students are expected to acquire in-depth understanding of the development, function and meaning of Buddhist art through studying archaeological and extant art and artefacts in their respective religious settings. They are also required to undertake independent research on selected topics at the end of the course.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. analyze important works of painting, sculpture, and architecture created by each Buddhist tradition in different parts of Asia;2. identify regional variances, trans-regional diffusions, inter-regional commonalities, and historical transformations among cultures of the pan-Buddhist world;3. recognize the function and meaning of key Buddhist art and artefacts in the religious settings;4. understand philosophy of Buddhism and its historical development;5. develop skills in writing academic essays.

title: Ancient Chinese Bronzes and Metal Art
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course provides an in-depth exploration of ancient Chinese bronzes, focusing on their artistic, technological, and cultural significance. Students will examine the featured research and scholarly debates surrounding the production, function, and iconography of these important artifacts from China’s remote past. Through a combination of lectures, discussions, and examination of museum objects, students will develop a nuanced understanding of the role of bronze in shaping China’s material culture and artistic traditions.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. gain a comprehensive understanding of ancient Chinese bronzes, exploring their artistic, technological, and cultural significance;2. develop critical analysis skills to appreciate the role of bronzes in affecting the development of Chinese culture, ritual, and civilization;3. act as active observers and thinkers, engaging thoughtfully with the artistic expressions found in ancient bronzes;4. acquire essential research skills that prepare students for advanced studies in art history, with a focus on ancient Chinese artifacts.

title: Art, Time, and Technology
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course introduces significant theories and case studies in media art history, spanning from the Enlightenment to the 21st century. The first part of the course will present an overview of the technological advancement in optical and sound media as well as their revival in the contemporary art scene. It will also provide theoretical frameworks for studying the aesthetics of moving image art, particularly the issues of temporality and performativity. The second part will focus on the development of the time-based media art in Asia. Topics and mediums discussed include the camera obscura, early film, intermedia installations, Net art, the digital turn, sound art, media art preservation, performance, and digital theatre. Class activities will include a visit to a local museum or archive, group discussions, and a presentation at the end of the semester. Drawing on key artworks and fundamental theories, it aims to guide students to explore how media-based practices evolved in various social environments responding to the history of technology, and develop research skills for academic writing and curating.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. identify the histories and theories of media art and moving image art in Asia;     2. elaborate on major media art movements from the Enlightenment to the 21st century;3. apply major theories of media art history to research papers and curatorial projects;                    4. identify key conservation issues of media art in museums;5. employ various approaches to analysing the analogue and digital media.
syllabus: Introduction to the Time-based Media: History, Mediums, ConceptsThis session explores the early history of time-based media and telecommunication art. There will also be an introduction on the formation of media art history as a discipline.The Materiality and Temporality of FilmTwo sessions will be devoted to the history of moving image, the documentation and representation of time in early time-based media, and the development of gallery film. PhotographyThis session will cope with the history and theory of photography, as well as how the digital turn impacted the photographic practice. Video and Interactive MediaThis session explores the development from analogue and digital video to multi-media installation. It will also discuss transnational networks of intermedia practice such as Fluxus. From Performativity to Digital TheatreTwo sessions will be devoted to the history of performance art and the liveness discourse, as well as an overview on the genealogy of digital theatre.Game Art and Net ArtThis session is devoted to the intersection of game art and video art. We will also discuss case studies of net art.  Data CapitalismThis session explores the concept of born-digital objects and conservation practices. It will also draw from Hito Steyerl’s creative works and critical writings to discuss data capitalism and problems resulted by data discrimination in the metaverse.Posthuman PositionsThis session is devoted to environmentalism in creative arts and live art.Media Art in AsiaTwo sessions will be devoted to the history of video art in China and Japan. A field trip to a local museum will be integrated.

title: English Writing Workshop
requirements: For students in MA Chinese Art History
description: This course is designed to help students develop their skills in writing about the history of Chinese art in English. Structured as a series of writing workshops, it introduces key forms of writing related to Chinese art, such as catalogue entries and academic articles. Through the introduction of art terminology, analysis of exemplary writing samples—including their organization and style—and guided writing exercises, students will acquire essential skills for articulating Chinese art history in different formats. The course also familiarizes students with specialized vocabulary related to different types of Chinese art objects, laying a strong foundation for future, in-depth research and writing on Chinese art history in English.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:1. become familiar with English terminology in major areas of Chinese art history;2. read and critically analyse art historical essays;3. identify key components and structure of art historical writings for different purposes;4. compose catalogue entries and an argumentative article on Chinese art objects in English.

description: Students who cannot complete the M.F.A. programme in two years’ time may take this course according to their length of study. This course will continue to provide students with guidance on their creative work as well as their written thesis.

title: History of Western Comics
description: (UGEC2317 is double-coded with FAAS2116.) This course traces the history of comics and graphic novels in Western Europe and North America. Beginning with an introduction presenting the main characteristics of this medium, this course will trace its development, from the beginnings of storytelling with images in Antiquity to the latest innovations. Even though they have retained their own characteristics over the last two centuries, Western European and North American comics have also developed in close proximity. Following the development of the press and book industry, as well as other media like cinema, comics and graphic novels have a rich history that can only be understood in their cultural context. This course is designed to allow students to understand how this medium has shaped and been shaped by many aspects of the history and cultures of these places.
outcome: After completing the course, students will be able to:  Know the development and changing status of comics and graphic novels within the wider history of Western Europe and North America;  identify how these changes took place and how they redefined comics and graphic novels in the present;  recognize the main artists of the medium, how they were influenced by their cultural context and how they also influenced it in return;  build informed opinion on the quality and relevance of the comics of the 20th and 21st century.  Develop skills in writing academic essays and speaking in public.
syllabus: Introduction: What is Sequential Art How to identify the characteristics of the medium know as ‘comics’  Why the concept of ‘sequential art’ is a more comprehensive way to define the medium of ‘comics’  How academic authors understand the notion of sequential art   Historical Precedents of Sequential Storytelling How comics in their modern form emerged from other art forms from the past  Origins of sequential story telling from Antiquity to the early 19th century   European Precursors How European precursors redefined sequential storytelling  Europe until the late 19th century: the main source of original comics  first full-fledged practitioner of this medium, Rodolphe Töpffer (1840-1846)  influence of other media on comics (in particular new printing technology and cinema)   North American Early Comics How full-fledged comics emerged in North America  Emigration of many artists to North America in the late 19th century  The comics strip in commercial context of the mass media (newspapers)   European Early Comics How comics became mainstream in Western Europe, from the beginning of the 20th century to the inter-war period.  Thriving publication industry that grew through specialization  Specialized for children and young persons  A few exceptions of more adult-oriented comics   North American Golden Age How comics grew to become a thriving global industry  The new superpower status of the United States gave to American comics a global reach  Mickey Mouse, Popeye the sailor become world-wide influences  The period sees the creation of an entire culture of superheroes symbolizing American global dominance in the realm of popular culture   European Golden Age Less globally influential at first, European comics also become globally significant  New European comics under the influence of North American culture  Other European comics developed as original creations that also enjoyed a global readership  Growth of a comics industry geared towards an adult readershop   North American Renaissance: Underground Comix How the North American counterculture redefined the medium of comics  End of the censorship on comics imposed in the 1950s  Expansion of the possibilities and public of the medium  Influence on the present   European Renaissance: the 1970s and beyond How both mainstream and counterculture began to expand the field of comics  More gradually than in North America, comics became a medium for an adult readership  Creation of many independent comics publishers and magazines  Growing literary ambitions of comics creators  Comics become an accepted field of academic research   Reshaping the Medium How the new directions initiated after the 1970s became a global explorations of new forms and contents  Comics become a highly literate field of artistic creation: the advent of the graphic novel  The influence of academic research on the medium  The influence of new technologies on comics creation

title: Art and Culture of Korea
description: (UGEC3309 is double-coded with FAAS3113.) This course—an interdisciplinary study of art history, archaeology, anthropology, and religious studies among others—introduces the visual and material culture of the Korean peninsula and its adjacent regions from the Neolithic Age to the early twentieth century CE by surveying major historic monuments and excavated artifacts. Major topics include (1) state formation, (2) tombs and mortuary furnishings, (3) the influx of Buddhism and its successful development, (4) capitals and provinces, (5) elite culture of the court, aristocrats, and the literati, (6) ceramics and lacquerware, and (7) trans-regional interaction, especially, with China and Japan.

title: Art and Culture of Japan
description: (UGEC3319 is double-coded with FAAS3114.) This course—an interdisciplinary study of art history, archaeology, anthropology, and religious studies—introduces the visual and material culture of the Japanese archipelago from the Prehistoric Age to the twentieth century by surveying major monuments and sites. Major topics include (1) prehistoric potteries, (2) tombs and mortuary furnishings, (3) the influx of Buddhism and its successful development, (4) capitals and provinces, (5) elite culture of the court, aristocrats, and the learned, (6) ceramics and lacquerware, and (7) trans-regional interaction, especially, with China and Korea.

title: Creative Workshop for Contemporary Chinese Art
description: This course was designed to bridge Chinese and Western Art through seminars and studio practice. Since the late 1970s, Chinese Art has experienced major breakthroughs and has provided new insights for the development of contemporary art worldwide. The course will therefore re-examine the existing resources of Chinese art and culture and incorporate them using the methodologies of contemporary art in order to create new directions for art practices. Elitist and popular Chinese arts will be reconsidered in order to combine them with a local character and, using the contemporary art methods mainly coming from the West, students will be encouraged to find their own creative directions.

title: Arts of Medieval China: Three Kingdoms through Five Dynasties
description: This course surveys the art and material culture of medieval China. The medieval or early medieval period spans between the fall of the Han (206 BCE-220 CE) and the establishment of the Song (960-1279). With primary reference to archaeological evidence discovered in the recent six decades, the course considers (1) cities and palaces; (2) tombs and ritual architecture; (3) trans-and intra-regional connections; (4) the rise of new artistic forms, media, and technologies; and (5) the spread of Buddhist visual culture and its impact to Chinese society.

title: Chinese and Western Comparative Aesthetics
description: Relying on famous examples from the Chinese and Western worlds and using several types of sources (literature, philosophy, poetry and the visual arts), this course is divided into two parts. The first part will compare and contrast two radically different conceptions of art. The second part will present the global revolution in thought that has led to today’s developments in the arts created by the Chinese people in Mainland China and abroad.
